1206: \begin{proof}
1207: On \(\Theta_{\varepsilon,M}\), both eigenvalues of the zero-labelled kernel
1208: are at most \(e^{-\varepsilon}\).  At a repeated eigenvalue its powers carry
1209: only a first-degree Jordan factor.  Hence, for constants independent of
1210: \(\theta\),
1211: \[
1212: \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{\varepsilon,M}}
1213: \PP_\theta(G\ge k)\le C(1+k)e^{-\varepsilon k},
1214: \qquad k\ge0.
1215: \]
1216: Every exponential moment of \(G\) of order below \(\varepsilon\) is
1217: therefore uniformly bounded.  The complete-cycle reward in Theorem~C is a
1218: function of two consecutive independent gaps, so the corresponding
1219: triangular arrays are \(1\)-dependent and have uniformly bounded fourth
1220: moments.  The usual even--odd blocking proof of the \(1\)-dependent CLT is
1221: then uniform along every convergent parameter sequence.  The renewal-count
1222: replacement and the two endpoint deletions are uniform by the same
1223: exponential bound.  Compactness and the subsequence criterion give the
1224: uniform bounded-Lipschitz CLT.  The maximal and Chernoff bounds in the proof
1225: of \Cref{lem:paper-level-separated-covariance-main} use only these uniform
1226: moment constants, so they also give the stated uniform covariance
1227: consistency.
1228: 
1229: It remains to prove nondegeneracy rather than assume it.  If
1230: \(c^\top\Sigma_rc=0\), put
1231: \[
1232: f(i,j)=c^\top
1233: \left[
1234: \begin{pmatrix}
1235: 1\\ \mathbf1_{\{i=0\}}\\
1236: \mathbf1_{\{i=1\}}+\mathbf1_{\{i=0,j=0\}}
1237: \end{pmatrix}
1238: -r(i+1)
1239: \right].
1240: \]
1241: For a full-support i.i.d. gap law, the Hoeffding row--column decomposition
1242: of a one-dependent sequence says that its long-run variance is zero exactly
1243: when \(f(i,j)=u_i-u_j\).  The degenerate interaction residual of \(f\) is
1244: \[
1245: c_2(\mathbf1_{\{i=0\}}-g_0)
1246: (\mathbf1_{\{j=0\}}-g_0).
1247: \]
1248: Since \(0<g_0<1\), vanishing of the interaction forces \(c_2=0\).  Then
1249: \(f\) depends only on \(i\), and an identity \(f(i)=u_i-u_j\) for all
1250: \(i,j\) forces \(f\equiv0\).  For all \(i\ge1\), this reads
1251: \[
1252: c_0-(c^\top r)(i+1)=0,
1253: \]
1254: so \(c^\top r=c_0=0\); the value \(i=0\) then gives \(c_1=0\).  Thus
1255: \(c=0\), and \(\Sigma_r\) is positive definite.  Its entries are continuous
1256: in \(\theta\) by dominated convergence.  Compactness and the rank-two
1257: conclusion of \Cref{prop:analytic-joint-image-chart-main} now give the
1258: uniform positive lower bound for \(\Omega=J\Sigma_rJ^\top\).
1259: 
1260: For any positive-definite
1261: \(\Omega=(\omega_{ij})_{i,j=1}^2\), direct completion of squares gives
1262: \[
1263: \inf_{u\ge0}
1264: \left\|\binom e{d-u}\right\|_{\Omega^{-1}}^2
1265: =\frac{e^2}{\omega_{11}}
1266: +\frac{\{d-(\omega_{12}/\omega_{11})e\}_{-}^2}
1267: {\omega_{22}-\omega_{12}^2/\omega_{11}}.
1268: \]
1269: Hence \(T_N\) is exactly the estimated covariance-metric distance to
1270: \(\{0\}\times[0,\infty)\).  Residualization makes its two Gaussian limits
1271: independent.  At a fixed interior point the standardized slack diverges to
1272: \(+\infty\), leaving one squared normal.  At the boundary it is centered,
1273: and conditioning on its sign gives the equal mixture of one and two degrees
1274: of freedom.
1275: 
1276: For uniform size, take an arbitrary null sequence and a convergent parameter
1277: subsequence.  If \(\eta_N\) is bounded, take a further subsequence on which
1278: it converges.  The sequential CLT gives the asserted limit, and
1279: \((z+\eta)^-\le z^-\) for \(\eta\ge0\) shows stochastic domination by the
1280: boundary law.  If \(\eta_N\to\infty\), its negative part vanishes in
1281: probability and \(c_{N,\alpha}\ge c_{1,\alpha}\), so the rejection
1282: probability has upper limit at most \(\alpha\).  The usual
1283: near-maximizing-sequence contradiction proves the displayed supremum bound.
1284: Finally, under the explicit alternative assumptions, the continuous mapping
1285: theorem makes \(N^{-1}T_N\) converge to the strictly positive squared
1286: distance from \(\psi(r)\) to the constraint cone, proving consistency.
1287: \end{proof}

1289: \begin{proposition}[Dominated renewal local power]
1290: \label{prop:joint-physical-image-local-power-main}
1291: Fix an exchange-diagonal physical point \(r_\circ\) in
1292: \(\Theta_{\varepsilon,M}\), and let \(g^\circ=(g_k^\circ)_{k\ge0}\) be its
1293: Palm gap law, with mean cycle length \(\mu^\circ\).  For
1294: \(\eta=(\eta_\mu,\eta_0,\eta_1)\), define
1295: \[
1296: g_\eta(k)=g^\circ(k)+v_\eta(k),
1297: \]
1298: where
1299: \[
1300: \begin{aligned}
1301: v_\eta(0)&=\eta_0,\\
1302: v_\eta(1)&=\eta_1,\\
1303: v_\eta(2)&=-\eta_\mu-3\eta_0-2\eta_1,\\
1304: v_\eta(3)&=\eta_\mu+2\eta_0+\eta_1,\\
1305: v_\eta(k)&=0,\qquad k\ge4.
1306: \end{aligned}
1307: \]
1308: On a sufficiently small fixed neighbourhood of the origin this is a
1309: full-support probability law.  The resulting stationary renewal experiment
1310: is differentiable in quadratic mean and locally asymptotically normal per
1311: unit calendar time, with information
1312: \[
1313: \mathcal I_{ij}
1314: =\frac1{\mu^\circ}\sum_{k=0}^3
1315: \frac{v_i(k)v_j(k)}{g_k^\circ},
1316: \]
1317: where \(v_i\) denotes the coefficient vector of the \(i\)-th component of
1318: \(\eta\).  The matrix \(\mathcal I\) is positive definite.
1319: 
1320: All first-order directions in three-inclusion space are represented by this
1321: experiment.  Indeed, for any renewal gap law,
1322: \[
1323: r=\left(\frac1\mu,\frac{g_0}{\mu},
1324: \frac{g_1+g_0^2}{\mu}\right),
1325: \]
1326: and the Jacobian with respect to \((\mu,g_0,g_1)\) is
1327: \[
1328: \begin{pmatrix}
1329: -\mu^{-2}&0&0\\
1330: -g_0\mu^{-2}&\mu^{-1}&0\\
1331: -(g_1+g_0^2)\mu^{-2}&2g_0\mu^{-1}&\mu^{-1}
1332: \end{pmatrix},
1333: \qquad \det=-\mu^{-4}\ne0.
1334: \]
1335: 
1336: Let a local sequence in this experiment satisfy
1337: \[
1338: \sqrt N\,e(r_N)\longrightarrow\delta,\qquad
1339: \sqrt N\,\mathcal D(r_N)\longrightarrow\tau.
1340: \]
1341: At \(r_\circ\), write
1342: \[
1343: \Omega=
1344: \begin{pmatrix}\omega_{11}&\omega_{12}\\
1345: \omega_{12}&\omega_{22}\end{pmatrix},
1346: \qquad
1347: \beta=\frac{\omega_{12}}{\omega_{11}},
1348: \qquad
1349: v=\omega_{22}-\frac{\omega_{12}^2}{\omega_{11}},
1350: \]
1351: and put
1352: \[
1353: a_*=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{\omega_{11}}},
1354: \qquad
1355: b_*=\frac{\tau-\beta\delta}{\sqrt v}.
1356: \]
1357: For the test in
1358: \Cref{thm:uniform-joint-physical-image-test-main},
1359: \[
1360: T_N\Rightarrow X^2+(Y^-)^2,
1361: \qquad
1362: X\sim N(a_*,1),\quad Y\sim N(b_*,1),
1363: \]
1364: with \(X\) and \(Y\) independent, and the boundary critical value is
1365: selected with probability tending to one.  Hence its complete local-power
1366: function is
1367: \[
1368: \pi_\alpha(\delta,\tau)
1369: =\PP\{X^2+(Y^-)^2>c_{\partial,\alpha}\}.
1370: \]
1371: For deterministic evaluation, define
1372: \[
1373: A(q,a)=\Phi_{\rm N}(\sqrt q-a)-\Phi_{\rm N}(-\sqrt q-a),
1374: \]
1375: where \(\Phi_{\rm N}\) and \(\phi_{\rm N}\) denote the standard normal
1376: distribution and density.  Then
1377: \[
1378: \begin{aligned}
1379: \pi_\alpha(\delta,\tau)
1380: =1&-\Phi_{\rm N}(b_*)A(c_{\partial,\alpha},a_*)\\
1381: &-\int_{-\sqrt{c_{\partial,\alpha}}}^{0}
1382: A(c_{\partial,\alpha}-y^2,a_*)\phi_{\rm N}(y-b_*)\,dy .
1383: \end{aligned}
1384: \]
1385: 
1386: In particular, a physical sequence satisfying
1387: \[
1388: N^{1/4}|p_N-s_N|\longrightarrow\xi
1389: \]
1390: has \((\delta,\tau)=(0,\xi^2)\), so
1391: \(\pi_\alpha(0,\xi^2)\le\alpha\).  Conversely, for every \(\xi>0\), the
1392: dominated renewal experiment contains a nonreal-root-side sequence with
1393: \((\delta,\tau)=(0,-\xi^2)\), and
1394: \[
1395: \pi_\alpha(0,-\xi^2)>\alpha.
1396: \]
1397: The restriction \(\xi>0\) is essential; at \(\xi=0\) the power equals
1398: \(\alpha\).
1399: 
1400: Finally, the null tangent cone and its first-order indistinguishable
1401: subspace are
1402: \[
1403: T_{H_0}(r_\circ)
1404: =\{h:De(r_\circ)h=0,\ D\mathcal D(r_\circ)h\ge0\},
1405: \]
1406: \[
1407: \ker D\psi(r_\circ)
1408: =\{h:De(r_\circ)h=0,\ D\mathcal D(r_\circ)h=0\}.
1409: \]
1410: Thus a direction with \(De\,h=0\) and \(D\mathcal D\,h>0\) is a physical
1411: interior direction whose root separation occurs at the
1412: \(N^{-1/4}\) scale; it is not model misspecification.
1413: \end{proposition}

1415: \begin{proof}
1416: The displayed coefficients satisfy
1417: \[
1418: \sum_kv_\eta(k)=0,\qquad
1419: \sum_k(k+1)v_\eta(k)=\eta_\mu,
1420: \]
1421: and change \(g_0,g_1\) by \(\eta_0,\eta_1\), respectively.  On the compact
1422: physical set, \(g_k^\circ\) is uniformly positive for \(0\le k\le3\);
1423: hence sufficiently small perturbations remain probability laws dominated by
1424: counting measure.  The one-cycle score is \(v_i(k)/g_k^\circ\).  The three
1425: coefficient vectors are linearly independent, which proves positive
1426: definiteness of \(\mathcal I\).  A Taylor expansion of the finite changed
1427: part of the one-cycle log likelihood gives quadratic-mean differentiability.
1428: The initial and terminal incomplete cycles contribute \(o_{\PP}(1)\) to the
1429: local log-likelihood ratio, while the number of complete cycles divided by
1430: \(N\) converges to \(1/\mu^\circ\).  The independent-cycle score CLT
1431: therefore proves the stated calendar-time LAN expansion.  This is the
1432: finite-support regenerative specialization of standard LAN theory
1433: \cite{vanDerVaart1998AsymptoticStatistics}.
1434: 
1435: The three moment identities and the nonzero Jacobian determinant prove local
1436: surjectivity onto inclusion space.  The rank-two constraint conclusion in
1437: \Cref{prop:analytic-joint-image-chart-main} then makes every pair
1438: \((\delta,\tau)\) locally attainable.
1439: 
1440: Under a \(N^{-1/2}\) local perturbation, the uniform studentization in
1441: \Cref{thm:uniform-joint-physical-image-test-main} and the third lemma give
1442: two residualized independent normals with the displayed means.  Since
1443: \(Z_{d,N}=O_{\PP}(1)\), the boundary critical value is selected.  To compute
1444: the acceptance probability, condition first on \(Y\ge0\), and then integrate
1445: over \(-\sqrt{c_{\partial,\alpha}}\le Y<0\); this gives the one-dimensional
1446: integral.
1447: 
1448: For a physical root pair,
1449: \(\mathcal D(r_N)=(p_N-s_N)^2\) and \(e(r_N)=0\), proving the physical-side
1450: claim.  On the nonreal side, \(b_*<0\) for \(\xi>0\).  Coupling
1451: \(Y=Z+b_*\) to the boundary variable \(Z\) shows that \(Y^-\) strictly
1452: stochastically exceeds \(Z^-\) on a set of positive probability, proving
1453: strictly greater power.  At \(\xi=0\) the laws coincide.  The tangent-cone
1454: formulas follow from the rank-two constraint qualification and the local
1455: description \(e=0,\mathcal D\ge0\).
1456: \end{proof}

1745: \begin{theorem}[Complete Markov--Palm tangent space and pointwise omnibus score]
1746: \label{thm:complete-markov-palm-tangent-omnibus-main}
1747: Fix $0<\alpha<1$, an interior exchange point $\theta_0=(x_0,x_0)$, and let
1748: $g=(g_k)_{k\geq0}$ be its Palm zero-gap law.  Thus $g_k>0$,
1749: $\mu=\sum_{k\geq0}(k+1)g_k<\infty$, and, for this sampled-counter law,
1750: $g$ has an exponential tail.  Put
1751: \[
1752:  \mathsf H=L^2(g\otimes g),\qquad
1753:  \mathsf H_{\rm int}=\{q\in\mathsf H:
1754:  \EE(q\mid G_0)=\EE(q\mid G_1)=0\},
1755: \]
1756: where $G_0,G_1$ are independent with law $g$, and define
1757: \[
1758:  \mathsf T=\{q\in\mathsf H_{\rm int}:q(0,0)=0\}.
1759:  \tag{H}
1760: \]
1761: Consider all quadratic-mean differentiable Markov-gap paths
1762: \[
1763:  Q_t(\ell\mid k)=g_\ell w_t(k,\ell),\qquad w_0=1,
1764:  \qquad \left\|\frac{2(\sqrt{w_t}-1)}t-q\right\|_{\mathsf H}
1765:  \longrightarrow0,
1766: \tag{I}
1767: \]
1768: whose rows sum to one, for which $gQ_t=g$, and which preserve
1769: $(r_0,r_1,r_2)$ to first order.  Then the following statements hold.
1770: 
1771: \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
1772: \item The closed tangent space of these paths is exactly $\mathsf T$; in
1773: particular it is infinite dimensional.  If
1774: \[
1775:  u_0(k)=\mathbf1_{\{k=0\}}-g_0,\qquad
1776:  v_0(k,\ell)=u_0(k)u_0(\ell),
1777: \]
1778: then
1779: \[
1780:  \mathsf T=\mathsf H_{\rm int}\ominus\operatorname{span}\{v_0\}.
1781:  \tag{J}
1782: \]
1783: Every $q\in\mathsf T$ is realized by a two-sided path in \textup{(I)} whose
1784: kernels satisfy a Doeblin minorization by $(1-o(1))g$ and preserve $g$ and
1785: all three inclusion coordinates exactly.  A nonzero such path is nonrenewal
1786: for all sufficiently small nonzero $t$.
1787: 
1788: \item Every adjacent-pair score generated by a quadratic-mean differentiable
1789: renewal marginal path belongs to the closed span of
1790: $s(G_0)+s(G_1)$, with $s\in L^2_0(g)$.  Hence the sampled-counter renewal
1791: nuisance space is orthogonal to $\mathsf T$.  On the ambient space
1792: $\mathsf H$, the efficient information operator for the Markov interaction
1793: is
1794: \[
1795:  \mathcal I_{\rm eff}=\mu^{-1}\Pi_{\mathsf T},
1796:  \tag{K}
1797: \]
1798: where
1799: \[
1800:  \Pi_{\mathsf T}f=f-\EE(f\mid G_0)-\EE(f\mid G_1)+\EE f
1801:  -\frac{\langle f,v_0\rangle_{\mathsf H}}
1802:  {\|v_0\|_{\mathsf H}^2}v_0.
1803:  \tag{L}
1804: \]
1805: In particular,
1806: \[
1807:  \ker\mathcal I_{\rm eff}
1808:  =\mathsf H_{\rm int}^{\perp}\oplus\operatorname{span}\{v_0\},
1809:  \qquad
1810:  \left.\mathcal I_{\rm eff}\right|_{\mathsf T}
1811:  =\mu^{-1}I_{\mathsf T}.
1812:  \tag{M}
1813: \]
1814: 
1815: \item Delete the two incomplete endpoint cycles from a stationary record and
1816: write its complete gaps as $G_1,\ldots,G_{K_N}$, where
1817: $K_N/N\to_P\mu^{-1}$.  For $q\in\mathsf T$, let
1818: \[
1819:  \Delta_N(q)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{K_N-1}q(G_i,G_{i+1}).
1820: \]
1821: For each fixed finite collection $q_1,\ldots,q_d\in\mathsf T$, the null
1822: joint limit is centred Gaussian with covariance
1823: \[
1824:  \lim_{N\to\infty}\operatorname{Cov}
1825:  \{\Delta_N(q_a),\Delta_N(q_b)\}
1826:  =\mu^{-1}\langle q_a,q_b\rangle_{\mathsf H}.
1827:  \tag{N}
1828: \]
1829: Along the realizing paths constructed in part~\textup{(i)}, or any other
1830: such path whose retained-record endpoint log likelihood is $o_{P_0}(1)$,
1831: the score $q$, evaluated at $t_N=N^{-1/2}$, satisfies
1832: \[
1833:  \log\frac{dP_{N,q}}{dP_{N,0}}
1834:  =\Delta_N(q)-\frac1{2\mu}\|q\|_{\mathsf H}^2+o_{P_0}(1).
1835:  \tag{O}
1836: \]
1837: Thus the limit is the isonormal process on $\mathsf T$ with covariance
1838: \textup{(N)}, rather than a $\mathsf T$-valued normal random element with
1839: identity covariance.  No uniform-LAN assertion over arbitrary norm-compact
1840: subsets of $\mathsf T$ is made.
1841: 
1842: \item Put
1843: \[
1844:  e_0(k)=\frac{\mathbf1_{\{k=0\}}-g_0}{\sqrt{g_0(1-g_0)}}
1845: \]
1846: and choose a bounded orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,\ldots$ of
1847: $L^2_0(g)\cap\{e_0\}^{\perp}$.  Enumerate
1848: \[
1849:  \{e_a\otimes e_b:a,b\geq0,\ (a,b)\neq(0,0)\}
1850:  =\{\phi_1,\phi_2,\ldots\};
1851: \]
1852: this is an orthonormal basis of $\mathsf T$.  Fix strictly positive weights
1853: $\lambda_j$ satisfying
1854: \[
1855:  \sum_{j\geq1}\lambda_j<\infty,
1856:  \qquad
1857:  \sum_{j\geq1}\lambda_j\|\phi_j\|_\infty^2<\infty,
1858:  \tag{P}
1859: \]
1860: and any deterministic $J_N\uparrow\infty$.  Put
1861: \[
1862:  \widehat\mu_N=
1863:  \begin{cases}
1864:  K_N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{K_N}(G_i+1),&K_N\geq1,\\
1865:  1,&K_N=0,
1866:  \end{cases}
1867: \]
1868: and define, when $K_N\geq2$,
1869: \[
1870:  Z_{j,N}=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat\mu_N}{N}}
1871:  \sum_{i=1}^{K_N-1}\phi_j(G_i,G_{i+1}),\qquad
1872:  Q_N=\sum_{j=1}^{J_N}\lambda_jZ_{j,N}^2,
1873:  \tag{Q}
1874: \]
1875: and put $Q_N=0$ otherwise.  If $\zeta_j$ are independent standard normals,
1876: then
1877: \[
1878:  Q_N\Rightarrow Q_0:=\sum_{j\geq1}\lambda_j\zeta_j^2.
1879:  \tag{R}
1880: \]
1881: Let $c_{\alpha,\lambda}$ be the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $Q_0$.  Under the
1882: local direction $q=\sum_jq_j\phi_j\in\mathsf T$ along one of the paths
1883: admitted in \textup{(O)},
1884: \[
1885:  Q_N\Rightarrow
1886:  \sum_{j\geq1}\lambda_j
1887:  \left(\zeta_j+\frac{q_j}{\sqrt\mu}\right)^2.
1888:  \tag{S}
1889: \]
1890: Consequently the test
1891: $\psi_N=\mathbf1_{\{Q_N>c_{\alpha,\lambda}\}}$ has limiting power strictly
1892: larger than $\alpha$ for every fixed $q\in\mathsf T\setminus\{0\}$.
1893: 
1894: \item The null calibration in \textup{(R)} is stable along the exchange
1895: boundary in the following explicit local sense.  Let
1896: $\sigma=(p+s,ps)$ be the symmetric sampled-counter coordinate and, for fixed
1897: $C<\infty$, let $\sigma_N$ range over null sequences satisfying
1898: \[
1899:  \|\sqrt N(\sigma_N-\sigma_0)\|\leq C.
1900:  \tag{T}
1901: \]
1902: Use in \textup{(Q)} the basis fixed at $\sigma_0$ and the displayed
1903: $\widehat\mu_N$.  Then
1904: \[
1905:  \sup_{\sigma_N:\,\textup{(T)}}
1906:  \left|\PP_{\sigma_N}(Q_N>c_{\alpha,\lambda})-\alpha\right|
1907:  \longrightarrow0.
1908:  \tag{U}
1909: \]
1910: This class includes exchange-root splittings
1911: $N^{1/4}|p_N-s_N|=O(1)$ provided their symmetric coordinates obey
1912: \textup{(T)}.
1913: \end{enumerate}
1914: 
1915: The algebraic assertions in parts~\textup{(i)}--\textup{(ii)} use only full
1916: support of $g$, finite $\mu$, and square-integrability of each local score.
1917: For the explicit realizing paths, the uniform density-ratio bound controls
1918: the endpoint terms in parts~\textup{(iii)}--\textup{(iv)}.  The
1919: sampled-counter exponential tail and analytic dependence on $\sigma$ are used
1920: in part~\textup{(v)} for its uniform triangular-array statement.  No claim
1921: that finite mean alone controls the endpoints of every quadratic-mean
1922: differentiable stationary-record path is made.
1923: 
1924: Generic basis tests of serial independence, Hilbert-space central limit
1925: theorems, and Gaussian-shift arguments are established methods
1926: \cite{SkaugTjostheim1993SerialIndependence,
1927: DedeckerMerlevede2003HilbertCLT,vanDerVaart1998AsymptoticStatistics}.
1928: The assertions here are restricted to the sampled-counter Markov--Palm
1929: interaction: the additional atom constraint in \textup{(H)}, its information
1930: projection, and the exchange-boundary calibration of \textup{(Q)}.
1931: \end{theorem}
1932: 
1933: \begin{proof}
1934: The row and stationary-marginal identities for \textup{(I)} are
1935: \[
1936:  \sum_\ell g_\ell w_t(k,\ell)=1,
1937:  \qquad
1938:  \sum_k g_kw_t(k,\ell)=1.
1939: \]
1940: Differentiating in quadratic mean gives the two conditional-mean constraints
1941: in \textup{(H)}.  Fixed $g$ fixes $r_0=\mu^{-1}$ and
1942: $r_1=\mu^{-1}g_0$, whereas a stationary Markov gap law satisfies
1943: \[
1944:  r_2=\mu^{-1}\{g_1+g_0Q_t(0\mid0)\}.
1945: \]
1946: Since point evaluation at $(0,0)$ is continuous in $\mathsf H$,
1947: $Q_t(0\mid0)=g_0\{1+tq(0,0)+o(t)\}$; hence preservation of $r_2$ to first
1948: order is equivalent to $q(0,0)=0$.
1949: 
1950: For $q\in\mathsf H_{\rm int}$, direct expansion and double centring give
1951: \[
1952:  \langle q,v_0\rangle_{\mathsf H}=g_0^2q(0,0),
1953: \]
1954: which proves \textup{(J)} and \textup{(L)}.  To prove realizability, truncate
1955: $q$ at levels $m$ and write
1956: $q_m=\Pi_{\mathsf T}\{(-m)\vee(q\wedge m)\}$.  Then $q_m$ is bounded and
1957: $q_m\to q$ in $\mathsf H$.  Choose $m(t)\uparrow\infty$ so slowly that
1958: $|t|\|q_{m(t)}\|_\infty\to0$ and set
1959: $w_t=1+tq_{m(t)}$.  Its weighted row and column sums are exactly one and
1960: $w_t(0,0)=1$; hence all three inclusion coordinates are exact.  Moreover,
1961: $Q_t(\ell\mid k)\geq\{1-o(1)\}g_\ell$, proving the Doeblin assertion.  If
1962: a nonzero score generated a renewal kernel, it would have the form
1963: $a(\ell)$; the two centring identities would then force $a=0$.
1964: The inequality
1965: \[
1966:  \left|2\{\sqrt{1+x}-1\}-x\right|\leq Cx^2,
1967:  \qquad |x|\leq\tfrac12,
1968: \]
1969: together with $|t|\|q_{m(t)}\|_\infty\to0$ proves the quadratic-mean
1970: differentiability in \textup{(I)}.
1971: 
1972: The Hoeffding row--column decomposition of $L^2(g\otimes g)$ is
1973: \[
1974:  \mathbb R\oplus L^2_0(G_0)\oplus L^2_0(G_1)
1975:  \oplus\mathsf H_{\rm int}.
1976: \]
1977: A renewal marginal perturbation contributes only its one-gap score at the two
1978: ends of an adjacent pair.  It is therefore orthogonal to $\mathsf T$.
1979: Under the null, successive interaction rewards have zero lag-one covariance:
1980: \[
1981:  \EE\{q_a(G_0,G_1)q_b(G_1,G_2)\}=0.
1982: \]
1983: The number of complete cycles per calendar bin tends to $\mu^{-1}$, so the
1984: information quadratic form is $\mu^{-1}\|q\|_{\mathsf H}^2$.  Projection
1985: onto the admissible interaction scores proves \textup{(K)}--\textup{(M)}.
1986: 
1987: For each fixed finite collection of scores, the one-dependent central limit
1988: theorem and random-index replacement prove \textup{(N)}.  For the realizing
1989: paths in part~\textup{(i)}, the bound
1990: $|t|\|q_{m(t)}\|_\infty\to0$ also makes the endpoint log likelihood
1991: negligible.  Quadratic-mean differentiability then gives \textup{(O)}; the
1992: same conclusion holds under the alternative endpoint hypothesis stated in
1993: part~\textup{(iii)}.  This proves the finite-dimensional local experiment.
1994: Identity covariance on the
1995: infinite-dimensional space is not trace class, so the limit can only be
1996: interpreted cylindrically as the displayed isonormal process.
1997: 
1998: The normalized $e_0$ is proportional to $u_0$.  Tensoring an orthonormal
1999: basis of $L^2_0(g)$ gives an orthonormal basis of
2000: $\mathsf H_{\rm int}$, and deleting $e_0\otimes e_0$ imposes \textup{(J)}.
2001: Condition \textup{(P)} makes
2002: \[
2003:  \bigl(\sqrt{\lambda_j}\phi_j(G_i,G_{i+1})\bigr)_{j\geq1}
2004: \]
2005: a square-integrable, one-dependent $\ell^2$-valued random variable.  Its
2006: lag-one covariance vanishes by double centring.  The Hilbert-space central
2007: limit theorem, random-index replacement, and truncation in $J_N$ therefore
2008: give \textup{(R)}.  Joint convergence with the likelihood score and the third
2009: lemma give \textup{(S)}.  If $q\neq0$, some $q_j\neq0$; for every positive
2010: threshold the square of a normal with nonzero mean strictly stochastically
2011: dominates a central normal square.  Conditioning on the remaining independent
2012: coordinates proves strict power because every $\lambda_j$ is positive.
2013: 
2014: Finally, analyticity of the sampled-counter gap law in the symmetric
2015: coordinate, together with its locally uniform exponential tail, gives,
2016: uniformly under \textup{(T)},
2017: \[
2018:  \frac{g_{\sigma_N}}g
2019:  =1+N^{-1/2}a_N+o(N^{-1/2})
2020:  \quad\hbox{in }L^2(g),
2021: \]
2022: with $(a_N)$ bounded.  Double centring cancels both linear terms, so for each
2023: $q\in\mathsf T$,
2024: \[
2025:  \EE_{g_{\sigma_N}\otimes g_{\sigma_N}}q
2026:  =N^{-1}\langle q,a_N\otimes a_N\rangle_{\mathsf H}+o(N^{-1}).
2027: \]
2028: The normalized score mean is therefore $o(1)$.  The second condition in
2029: \textup{(P)} supplies a common bounded envelope for the weighted feature,
2030: and the same expansion gives convergence of its covariance operator in trace
2031: norm.  The triangular-array Hilbert-space central limit theorem now yields
2032: \textup{(U)}.  Since the discriminant is $(p-s)^2$, the final inclusion of
2033: the $N^{-1/4}$ root-splitting sequences follows.
2034: \end{proof}

2036: \begin{proposition}[Exchange-point Helmert coupling bracket]
2037: \label{prop:helmert-growing-layer-bracket-main}
2038: Retain the exchange-point notation of
2039: \Cref{thm:complete-markov-palm-tangent-omnibus-main}, put
2040: $p_0=e^{-x_0}$, and write
2041: \[
2042:  S_j=\PP_g(G\geq j)=p_0^j(1+x_0j),\qquad j\geq0.
2043: \]
2044: For $j\geq0$ define the weighted Helmert contrast
2045: \[
2046:  e_j(k)=
2047:  \sqrt{\frac{S_{j+1}}{g_jS_j}}\,\mathbf1_{\{k=j\}}
2048:  -\sqrt{\frac{g_j}{S_jS_{j+1}}}\,\mathbf1_{\{k\geq j+1\}}.
2049:  \tag{V}
2050: \]
2051: Thus $e_0$ is the contrast used in
2052: \Cref{thm:complete-markov-palm-tangent-omnibus-main}, and
2053: $e_0,e_1,\ldots$ is an orthonormal basis of $L^2_0(g)$.  For $J\geq1$ let
2054: \[
2055:  \boldsymbol\Phi_J=
2056:  \bigl(e_a\otimes e_b:0\leq a,b\leq J,\ (a,b)\neq(0,0)\bigr),
2057:  \qquad d_J=(J+1)^2-1,
2058:  \tag{W}
2059: \]
2060: in any fixed order, and let $\mathbf Z_{J,N}$ be the corresponding vector of
2061: scores in \textup{(Q)}, with the basis in \textup{(V)} fixed at $\theta_0$.
2062: Set $n_N=N/\mu$.
2063: 
2064: If $J_N\to\infty$ and
2065: \[
2066:  \frac{d_{J_N}}{\sqrt{n_N}\,S_{J_N}}\longrightarrow0,
2067:  \tag{$X_{\rm suff}$}
2068: \]
2069: then, on extensions of the underlying probability spaces, there are
2070: $\boldsymbol\xi_N\sim\mathcal N(0,I_{d_{J_N}})$ such that
2071: \[
2072:  \|\mathbf Z_{J_N,N}-\boldsymbol\xi_N\|_2=o_{P_0}(1).
2073:  \tag{Y}
2074: \]
2075: This holds at the fixed exchange point $\theta_0$ and uniformly along the local
2076: sampled-counter null sequences in \textup{(T)}.  Conversely, \textup{(Y)} at
2077: $\theta_0$ implies the necessary condition
2078: \[
2079:  n_NS_{J_N}^2\longrightarrow\infty.
2080:  \tag{$X_{\rm nec}$}
2081: \]
2082: No sufficiency claim under \textup{($X_{\rm nec}$)} alone is made.  Closing the
2083: gap between \textup{($X_{\rm suff}$)} and \textup{($X_{\rm nec}$)} is an open
2084: interface: the general Euclidean Yurinskii bound used here retains an ambient
2085: dimension factor.
2086: 
2087: Replacing the deterministic cycle count by the
2088: calendar stopping index and replacing $\mu$ by $\widehat\mu_N$ contribute,
2089: respectively,
2090: \[
2091:  O_P(J_NN^{-1/4})\quad\hbox{and}\quad O_P(J_NN^{-1/2})
2092:  \tag{Z}
2093: \]
2094: in Euclidean norm.  The local null covariance perturbation contributes
2095: $O_P(J_N^3N^{-1/2})$; all three terms are $o_P(1)$ under
2096: \textup{($X_{\rm suff}$)}.
2097: 
2098: The necessity in \textup{($X_{\rm nec}$)} already follows from the fact that a standard
2099: Gaussian limit for the moving corner coordinate
2100: $e_{J_N}\otimes e_{J_N}$ requires
2101: \[
2102:  n_NS_{J_N}^2\longrightarrow\infty.
2103:  \tag{AA}
2104: \]
2105: More strongly, if some $r_N<J_N$ satisfies
2106: $n_NS_{r_N}^2\to0$ and $J_N-r_N\asymp J_N$, then, with probability tending
2107: to one, every score in the block
2108: \[
2109:  \{e_a\otimes e_b:r_N\leq a,b\leq J_N\}
2110:  \tag{AB}
2111: \]
2112: is zero.  The corresponding standard Gaussian block has
2113: $(J_N-r_N+1)^2$ degrees of freedom, so neither an unweighted chi-square
2114: approximation for that block nor an $o_P(1)$ Euclidean coupling can hold.
2115: 
2116: Both sides of the bracket have first-order layer constant $(2x_0)^{-1}$, but
2117: their second-order terms differ.  For any $\omega_N\to\infty$, a sufficient
2118: region is
2119: \[
2120:  J_N\leq
2121:  \frac{\log n_N-2\log\log n_N-\omega_N}{2x_0},
2122:  \tag{AC$_{\rm suff}$}
2123: \]
2124: whereas coupling requires
2125: \[
2126:  J_N\leq
2127:  \frac{\log n_N+2\log\log n_N-\omega_N}{2x_0}
2128:  \tag{AC$_{\rm nec}$}
2129: \]
2130: for some diverging $\omega_N$.
2131: If
2132: $2x_0J_N=\log n_N+2\log\log n_N-c+o(1)$ for a fixed $c\in\mathbb R$, then
2133: $n_NS_{J_N}^2\to e^c/4$, so \textup{(Y)} fails.  The previously verified
2134: sufficient region is therefore separated from the necessary boundary by a
2135: $4\log\log n_N$ window.  No assertion of sharpness or Le Cam equivalence is
2136: made.
2137: \end{proposition}
2138: 
2139: \begin{proof}
2140: The equal-rate dictionary gives the displayed formula for $S_j$.
2141: The two values in \textup{(V)} have weighted mean zero and weighted squared
2142: norm one.  Nested supports then give
2143: $\langle e_j,e_k\rangle_{L^2(g)}=0$ for $j\neq k$; completeness follows by
2144: successively separating the atoms $0,1,\ldots$ from the remaining tail.
2145: Since $S_{j+1}/S_j\to p_0$ and $g_j/S_j\to1-p_0$,
2146: \[
2147:  \|e_j\|_\infty\asymp S_j^{-1/2},\qquad
2148:  \max_{a,b\leq J}\|e_a\otimes e_b\|_\infty\asymp S_J^{-1}.
2149:  \tag{1}
2150: \]
2151: 
2152: For the deterministic-cycle argument, let
2153: $K_J(k)=\sum_{a=0}^Je_a(k)^2$.  Adding the constant function to the Helmert
2154: contrasts gives the projection onto the partition
2155: $\{0\},\ldots,\{J\},\{J+1,J+2,\ldots\}$; hence
2156: \[
2157:  1+K_J(k)=
2158:  \begin{cases}
2159:   g_k^{-1},&0\leq k\leq J,\\
2160:   S_{J+1}^{-1},&k\geq J+1.
2161:  \end{cases}
2162:  \tag{2}
2163: \]
2164: The equal-rate exponential tail and \textup{(2)} imply
2165: \[
2166:  \EE K_J(G)^{3/2}\leq C S_J^{-1/2},\qquad
2167:  \EE K_J(G)^2\leq C S_J^{-1}.
2168:  \tag{3}
2169: \]
2170: Thus, for the vector $\boldsymbol\Phi_J(G_i,G_{i+1})$, independence of the
2171: two gaps yields
2172: \[
2173:  \EE\|\boldsymbol\Phi_J(G_i,G_{i+1})\|_2^3\leq C S_J^{-1}.
2174:  \tag{4}
2175: \]
2176: We now prove the fixed exchange-point sufficiency.  Write $m=J+1$, let
2177: $P_J:\mathbb R^{m^2}\to\mathbb R^{d_J}$ delete the $e_0\otimes e_0$
2178: coordinate, and set
2179: \[
2180:  h_J(G)=(e_0(G),\ldots,e_J(G))^\top,
2181:  \qquad
2182:  Y_{i,J}=P_J\{h_J(G_i)\otimes h_J(G_{i+1})\}.
2183:  \tag{B1}
2184: \]
2185: Then $\EE Y_{i,J}=0$ and
2186: $\EE(Y_{i,J}Y_{i,J}^\top)=I_{d_J}$.  Moreover, double centring gives, for
2187: all retained coordinates,
2188: \[
2189:  \EE\{e_a(G_i)e_b(G_{i+1})e_c(G_{i+1})e_d(G_{i+2})\}=0.
2190:  \tag{B2}
2191: \]
2192: Thus distinct $Y_{i,J}$ are uncorrelated, and they are independent when their
2193: indices differ by more than one.
2194: 
2195: Put $n=\lfloor n_N\rfloor$ and
2196: $L=\lceil d_J^2+\log n\rceil$.  Partition the edge indices into consecutive
2197: blocks of length at most $L$, deleting one connecting edge between successive
2198: blocks.  The retained block sums are independent because their underlying
2199: gap sets are disjoint.  If $I$ and $D$ denote the retained and deleted edge
2200: sets, respectively, then
2201: \[
2202:  r:=|D|\leq \frac{n}{L+1}+L+1,
2203:  \qquad
2204:  \EE\left\|\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i\in D}Y_{i,J}\right\|_2^2
2205:  =\frac{rd_J}{n}
2206:  \leq C\left(\frac{d_J}{L}+\frac{Ld_J}{n}\right)=o(1).
2207:  \tag{B3}
2208: \]
2209: For a retained block $B$, split its edges by parity.  Each parity class is
2210: independent, so the Hilbert-space Rosenthal--Burkholder inequality
2211: \cite{Pinelis1994OptimalMartingaleBounds}, together with \textup{(4)}, yields
2212: \[
2213:  \EE\left\|\sum_{i\in B}Y_{i,J}\right\|_2^3
2214:  \leq C\{(Ld_J)^{3/2}+L/S_J\}.
2215:  \tag{B4}
2216: \]
2217: Let $\mathcal B$ be the retained blocks, put
2218: $X_B=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in B}Y_{i,J}$, and let
2219: $V_B=(|B|/n)I_{d_J}$ be its covariance.  For independent
2220: $Z_B\sim\mathcal N(0,I_{d_J})$, the second-order moment quantity in
2221: CMU's Corollary~2.3 is
2222: \[
2223:  \widetilde\beta_N
2224:  :=\sum_{B\in\mathcal B}\EE\{\|X_B\|_2^3
2225:        +\|V_B^{1/2}Z_B\|_2^3\}
2226:  \leq C\left\{
2227:   \frac{\sqrt L\,d_J^{3/2}}{\sqrt n}
2228:   +\frac1{\sqrt n\,S_J}
2229:  \right\}.
2230:  \tag{B5}
2231: \]
2232: Here the first summand follows from \textup{(B4)}.  For the Gaussian summand,
2233: $\EE\|Z_B\|_2^3\leq C d_J^{3/2}$ and
2234: $\sum_{B\in\mathcal B}|B|^{3/2}\leq\sqrt L\,n$, giving the same first
2235: order.  This Gaussian comparison contribution is part of the cited theorem
2236: and cannot be omitted.
2237: 
2238: We use the independent-vector Euclidean Yurinskii theorem in CMU's
2239: Corollary~2.3 \cite{CattaneoMasiniUnderwood2025Yurinskii}.
2240: Since $\phi_2(d_J)^2=2d_J$, it gives for every $\eta>0$ a coupling of the retained sum
2241: $A=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in I}Y_{i,J}$ to
2242: $T\sim\mathcal N(0,cI_{d_J})$, $c=|I|/n$, satisfying
2243: \[
2244:  \PP(\|A-T\|_2>\eta)
2245:  \leq24\left(\frac{2d_J\widetilde\beta_N}{\eta^3}\right)^{1/3}.
2246:  \tag{B6}
2247: \]
2248: Under \textup{($X_{\rm suff}$)}, $J=O(\log n)$ and
2249: \[
2250:  d_J\widetilde\beta_N
2251:  \leq C\left\{
2252:  \frac{\sqrt L\,d_J^{5/2}}{\sqrt n}
2253:  +\frac{d_J}{\sqrt n\,S_J}\right\}=o(1);
2254: \]
2255: the first term is $O((\log n)^7/\sqrt n)$ and the second is exactly the
2256: condition \textup{($X_{\rm suff}$)}, up to replacing $n_N$ by $n$.
2257: Put $q_N=2d_J\widetilde\beta_N$ and choose the coupling in \textup{(B6)}
2258: with $\eta_N=q_N^{1/6}$.  Then $\eta_N\to0$ and
2259: \[
2260:  \PP(\|A-T\|_2>\eta_N)\leq24q_N^{1/6}\longrightarrow0.
2261: \]
2262: This explicit diagonal choice is needed because the coupling variable in the
2263: cited theorem depends on the requested tolerance; it proves
2264: $\|A-T\|_2=o_P(1)$.  The covariance is exactly $cI_{d_J}$ by
2265: \textup{(B2)}.  If $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_{d_J})$ is independent of $T$, then
2266: \[
2267:  \xi=T+\sqrt{1-c}\,Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_{d_J}),
2268:  \qquad
2269:  \EE\|\xi-T\|_2^2=(1-c)d_J=\frac{rd_J}{n}=o(1).
2270:  \tag{B7}
2271: \]
2272: Combining \textup{(B3)}--\textup{(B7)} proves the deterministic-cycle
2273: exchange-point coupling under \textup{($X_{\rm suff}$)}.
2274: 
2275: For completeness, the uniform local-null result under
2276: \textup{($X_{\rm suff}$)} follows by retaining the direct martingale argument.
2277: The vectors in \textup{(B1)} are martingale differences for the filtration
2278: ending at $G_{i+1}$.  If $V_i$ denotes the conditional covariance of the
2279: $i$th normalized increment, then its block form and \textup{(2)} give
2280: \[
2281:  \EE\left\|\sum_{i\leq n_N}V_i-I_{d_J}\right\|_{\rm op}
2282:  \leq
2283:  \left\{\EE\left\|\sum_{i\leq n_N}V_i-I_{d_J}\right\|_{\rm F}^2\right\}^{1/2}
2284:  \leq C\sqrt{\frac{J}{n_NS_J}}.
2285:  \tag{5}
2286: \]
2287: Here the last inequality uses
2288: $\|e(G)e(G)^\top\|_{\rm F}^2=K_J(G)^2$ and the second bound in
2289: \textup{(3)}.  The ordinary martingale Yurinskii quantity is
2290: $O((\sqrt{n_N}S_J)^{-1})$ by \textup{(4)}.  Since the Euclidean Gaussian
2291: norm factor is of order $\sqrt{d_J}$, condition
2292: \textup{($X_{\rm suff}$)} makes both the Yurinskii term
2293: $d_J/(\sqrt{n_N}S_J)$ and the conditional-covariance term
2294: $d_J\sqrt{J/(n_NS_J)}$ tend to zero.  Therefore
2295: CMU's Corollary~2.2
2296: \cite{CattaneoMasiniUnderwood2025Yurinskii} gives \textup{(Y)} under
2297: \textup{($X_{\rm suff}$)}, uniformly after the perturbation below.  Choosing
2298: the coupling tolerance by the same deterministic diagonal argument makes this
2299: a single uniform $o_P(1)$ coupling sequence.
2300: 
2301: The renewal central limit theorem gives
2302: $K_N-n_N=O_P(\sqrt N)$.  A Hilbert-space martingale maximal inequality over
2303: that random terminal window gives squared Euclidean error
2304: $O_P(d_J/\sqrt N)$ after normalization, which is the square of the first
2305: order in
2306: \textup{(Z)}.  The usual root-$N$ consistency of $\widehat\mu_N$ gives the
2307: second.  It remains to make the triangular local-null comparison explicit.
2308: Let $\mathcal P_J$ be the partition in \textup{(2)} and let
2309: $g_N=g_{\sigma_N}$.  Analytic differentiation of the exact sampled-counter
2310: atom and tail formulae at the exchange point gives, uniformly under
2311: \textup{(T)} and for $J=O(\log N)$,
2312: \[
2313:  \max_{C\in\mathcal P_J}
2314:  \left|\frac{g_N(C)}{g(C)}-1\right|
2315:  \leq C N^{-1/2}(1+J^2).
2316:  \tag{6}
2317: \]
2318: For the singleton cells this follows from the density-ratio derivatives,
2319: which are $O(1+k^2)$ for $k\leq J$; for the final tail cell it follows by
2320: differentiating the closed tail formula before taking the ratio.  Every
2321: coordinate in \textup{(W)} is constant on each product cell of
2322: $\mathcal P_J\otimes\mathcal P_J$.  Consequently \textup{(6)} implies
2323: \[
2324:  \|\Sigma_{J,N}-I_{d_J}\|_{\rm op}=O(J^2N^{-1/2}),
2325:  \tag{7}
2326: \]
2327: where $\Sigma_{J,N}$ is the score covariance under $g_N$.  Moreover, if
2328: $u_{a,N}=\EE_{g_N}e_a$, double centring under $g$ gives
2329: \[
2330:  \left\|(u_{a,N}u_{b,N})_{(a,b)\neq(0,0)}\right\|_2
2331:  \leq\sum_{a=0}^J u_{a,N}^2=O(N^{-1}),
2332:  \tag{8}
2333: \]
2334: so the normalized score mean is $O(N^{-1/2})$.  Coupling
2335: $\Sigma_{J,N}^{1/2}\boldsymbol\xi_N$ and $\boldsymbol\xi_N$ with the same
2336: standard Gaussian vector, \textup{(7)} and the square-root perturbation
2337: bound give
2338: \[
2339:  \|(\Sigma_{J,N}^{1/2}-I)\boldsymbol\xi_N\|_2
2340:  =O_P(\sqrt{d_J}J^2N^{-1/2})=O_P(J^3N^{-1/2}).
2341:  \tag{9}
2342: \]
2343: Condition \textup{($X_{\rm suff}$)} implies $J_N=O(\log N)$.  Hence the
2344: deterministic-cycle block coupling and the two stopping terms prove
2345: \textup{(Y)} at the exchange point, whereas \textup{(6)}--\textup{(9)} and
2346: the martingale coupling prove the uniform local-null statement, both under
2347: \textup{($X_{\rm suff}$)}.
2348: 
2349: The corner contrast is nonzero exactly when both gaps are at least $J$.
2350: On that event its magnitude is bounded above and below by constant multiples
2351: of $S_J^{-1}$, by \textup{(1)}.  Its triangular-array Lindeberg condition is
2352: therefore exactly $\sqrt{n_N}S_{J_N}\to\infty$, which is \textup{(AA)}.
2353: If this fails along a subsequence, the number of nonzero corner summands has
2354: a nonvanishing atom at zero (and is asymptotically Poisson whenever
2355: $n_NS_{J_N}^2$ has a finite positive limit), excluding a standard normal
2356: limit.  For \textup{(AB)}, the expected number of adjacent pairs with both
2357: gaps at least $r_N$ is $O(n_NS_{r_N}^2)=o(1)$.  Markov's inequality proves
2358: the zero-block assertion, and the Gaussian comparison follows from its
2359: chi-square block energy.
2360: 
2361: Finally,
2362: \[
2363:  \log(n_NS_{J_N}^2)
2364:  =\log n_N-2x_0J_N+2\log(1+x_0J_N).
2365:  \tag{10}
2366: \]
2367: If \textup{($X_{\rm nec}$)} is near its maximal band, then
2368: $J_N\asymp\log n_N$ and
2369: $2\log(1+x_0J_N)=2\log\log n_N-2\log2+o(1)$.
2370: This proves the necessary region \textup{(AC$_{\rm nec}$)}.  Similarly,
2371: \[
2372:  \log\frac{d_{J_N}}{\sqrt{n_N}S_{J_N}}
2373:  =\log d_{J_N}-\tfrac12\log n_N+x_0J_N
2374:    -\log(1+x_0J_N),
2375: \]
2376: which gives \textup{(AC$_{\rm suff}$)}.  Under the critical scaling displayed
2377: in the proposition, \textup{(10)} converges to $c-2\log2$, which gives
2378: $n_NS_{J_N}^2\to e^c/4$.  The two calculations leave the stated
2379: $4\log\log n_N$ window unresolved.
2380: \end{proof}

           NON-IDENTIFIABILITY OF THE TWO STATE MARKOVIAN
                                       ARRIVAL PROCESS

                        Pepa RamÃ­rez1, Rosa E. Lillo2 and Michael P. Wiper3

Abstract
In this paper we consider the problem of identifiability of the two-state Markovian
Arrival process (MAP2). In particular, we show that the MAP2 is not identifiable and
conditions are given under which two different sets of parameters, induce identical
stationary laws for the observable process.

Keywords: Batch Markovian Arrival process, Markov Renewal process, Hidden
Markov models, Identifiability problems.

1 Corresponding author: Pepa RamÃ­rez, DÃ©partement Images et Signaux, UMR CNRS 5216, 961 rue de la
Houille Blanche, 38402 Saint Martin d'HÃ¨res Cedex, France.
E-mail: Pepa.Ramirezcobo@gipsa-lab.inpg.fr
2 Rosa E. Lillo, Universidad Carlos III, Departamento de EstadÃ­stica, e-mail: lillo@est-econ.uc3m.es
3Michael P. Wiper, Universidad Carlos III, Departamento de EstadÃ­stica,e-mail: mwiper@est-
econ.uc3m.es
2                   Ramirez et al.

   1. Introduction

   The Markovian arrival process (MAP) was defined in [10] and [9] as a generalization
of the Poisson arrival process allowing for both dependence between arrivals and non-
exponentially distributed interarrival times. The MAP is defined by two Markov
processes: the first counts the number of arrivals and the second, an underlying Markov
process, governs the state changes. At the end of a transition in a MAP an arrival
may or may not occur and although the transition holding times are exponentially
distributed, the interarrival times do not follow an exponential distribution. Special
cases of the MAP are the phase type renewal processes (which include both Erlang
and hyperexponential renewal process) and non-renewal processes such as the Markov
modulated Poisson process (MMPP). Stationary MAPs are dense in the family of all
stationary point processes; see [1]. Another important property of MAPs is that the
superposition of independent MAPs is again a MAP.

   The MAP is an challenging process from both a theoretical and applied points of
view. From a theoretical perspective, the queueing system where the MAP governs the
arrival process has been widely studied in the literature, combined with matrix analytic
methods (see for example [8]). On the other hand, the MAP has been proposed in the
literature as a suitable process for modeling teletraffic data, see e.g. [4], [5], [11], [6],
and [17]. In this case, the MAP is used to fit data where only the interarrival times
are observed and neither the underlying Markov chain nor the individual exponential
holding times are available and thus, the observed arrival process is a hidden Markov
process.

   When dealing with inference for hidden Markov processes, it is very common to
encounter identifiability problems which imply that the likelihood function does not
possess a unique maximum. Identifiability conditions for general, hidden Markov
processes are studied in [7] and [13]. Identifiability of the MMPP, was undertaken in
[15]. However, for the MAP, to the best of our knowledge, the identifiability problem
is still essentially unsolved.

   In this paper we address the problem of identifiability of the two-state MAP, or
MAP2. We conclude that, on the contrary to the MMPP, which is identifiable (see
[15]), the MAP2 is not identifiable.
Non-identifiability of the MAP2                             3

   The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we introduce the MAP and its
main properties. In Section 3, we study when two MAP2s have the same interarrival
time distributions, a necessary condition for non-identifiability. We call this property
weak equivalence. In Section 4 we consider the joint distribution of a sequence of
interarrival times generated from the MAP2 and show that there are at least two
different parameterizations of the MAP2 giving rise to the same joint distribution,
thus proving the non-identifiability of the MAP2. Finally in Section 5 we provide
conclusions and various possible extensions of this work.

2. The MAP and its main properties

   Consider an irreducible, continuous, Markov process J(t) with state space S =
{1, . . . , m} and generator matrix D. Let N (t) represent the cumulative number of
arrivals in (0, t]. A MAP, represented by {J(t), N (t)} behaves as follows: the initial
state i0  S is generated according to an initial probability vector  = (1, . . . , m)
and at the end of an exponentially distributed sojourn time in state i, with mean 1/i,
two possible state transitions can occur. Firstly, with probability 0  pij1  1 a single
arrival occurs and the MAP enters a state j  S, which may be the same as (j = i) or
different from (j = i) the previous state. Secondly, with probability 0  pij0  1, no
arrival occurs and the MAP enters a different state j = i. Given that from all states
a transition must occur to a different state without an arrival or to any state with an
arrival, then for 1  i  m,

                                 m        m

                                          pij0 + pij1 = 1.

                                 j=1,j=i  j=1

   When m = 2, we have a two state MAP, denoted by MAP2. Figure 1 illustrates
the different movements that can occur transitions that in this process by means of a
transition diagram.

   Define the matrices P0 = (pij0)i,jS and P1 = (pij1)i,jS where pii0 = 0. Then the
MAP is defined by the set {, , P0, P1}, where  = (1, . . . , m). Alternatively, the
MAP can be characterized by the rate matrices, D0 = (dij0)i,jS and D1 = (dij1)i,jS ,
where dii0 = -i, dij0 = ipij0, for j = i and dij1 = ipij1, for 1  i, j  m. This
definition implies that D  D0 + D1 is the infinitesimal generator of the underlying

                                         3. Weak equivalence

   There have been a number of examples of fitting the MMPP to internet data traces.
In most applications, the two-state case has been considered (see for example [16], [14]
or [3]). The MMPPs, despite being simplified MAPs (the matrix P1 is diagonal, and
thus they are characterized by two less parameters), are complex processes and usually,
two states, at most three, are enough to capture the data behavior.

   When modeling real data, usually just the times between arrivals are observed, and

they are weakly equivalent.

The term weak is employed because equivalence is expressed in a marginal sense. Since
the interarrival times in a MAP2 are not independent, condition (3.3) is necessary but
insufficient for non-identifiability. A general condition looking at the joint density of
the sequence of interarrival times is analyzed in Section 4.

\section{Bibliographic boundary for the theorem comparison}\label{app:supplementary-bibliographic-boundary}

The main article's compact theorem comparison separates direct theorem inputs,
nearby mathematical comparators, and contextual partial-observation literature.
Zamparo's renewal-binary process \cite{Zamparo2022RenewalBinary} is the direct
probability comparator for the renewal representation and CLT input.  MAP
background includes Neuts' Markovian point process
\cite{Neuts1979MAP}, Lucantoni's batch-MAP work
\cite{Lucantoni1991BMAP}, the non-renewal arrival process of
Lucantoni--Meier-Hellstern--Neuts
\cite{LucantoniMeierHellsternNeuts1990Vacations}, and the discrete-time MAP
construction of Alfa--Neuts \cite{AlfaNeuts1995DMAP}.  Recent structured-MAP
moment identities \cite{AsanjaraniHautphenneNazarathy2026StructuredMAPMoments}
are close to the moment calculations but do not contain the visible-renewal
quotient inverse.

MAP2 and phase-type nonidentifiability
\cite{RamirezCoboLilloWiper2010MAP2Nonidentifiability,
OCinneide1989PhaseTypeNonuniqueness} give the cautionary background for
hidden-label nonidentifiability.  Recent partial-observation papers
\cite{BauerSeifertVanderMeer2025Stroboscopic,
HarunariDuttaPolettiniRoldan2022VisibleTransitions,
VanDerMeerErtelSeifert2022TransitionWTD,
VanDerMeerDeguntherSeifert2023Snippets,ErtelSeifert2024BlurredTransitions,
VanDerMeerSaito2025FaultyCoarseGraining,
FritzErtelSeifert2025ImperfectObservations,
MaierHaslerSeifert2026Blackouts,GhosalBisker2022PartialLangevin,
DiTerlizziEtAl2024VarianceSumRule} provide physics-math context for partial
observability, variance diagnostics, and thermodynamic inference; they do not
prove the three-inclusion quotient inverse or the exchange-diagonal
certificate.

NUMERICAL CONCLUSION
- the complete physical n=2 Markovian fibre is the exact q interval
  between 1 and gamma/recovery, with rate-swapped physical endpoints.
- strict fibre-interior positivity holds off diagonal; the equal-rate
  interval collapses to the singleton q=1.
- physical n=2 inclusion triples satisfy the exact scalar image equation.
- the hidden-mode grid respects the sharp lower bound -exp(-2).
- the sampled-cycle mean agrees with the expansion through order delta^4.
- n=2: the known three-inclusion inverse recovers the unordered rate pair.
- n=2,3,4 serial subclasses: the confluent Hankel recurrence recovers
  the unordered sampled-pole multiset, including repeated poles.
- unrestricted killed-reset kernels: explicit reset-preserving similarity
  pairs have identical visible laws but different hidden kernels for n=2,3,4.
- pole collision is an ill-conditioning/singular-chart boundary, not an
  identifiability boundary; the exact boundary is the Markovian orbit fibre.

1. **HEADLINE RESULT.** **Complete two-state fibre arc and exchange dichotomy** (`thm:two-state-complete-fibre-arc-main`): for the physical two-state killed-reset kernel \(K\), its entire Markovian visible-law fibre is the arc \(\{M_q^{-1}KM_q:q\in[\min(1,\Gamma/\kappa_{\mathrm r}),\max(1,\Gamma/\kappa_{\mathrm r})]\}\), whose endpoints exchange the two rates and which is a singleton exactly when \(\Gamma=\kappa_{\mathrm r}\).

2. **IS IT ACTUALLY NEW? INCREMENTAL.** Ramírez-Cobo, Lillo and Wiper, “Nonidentifiability of the Two-State Markovian Arrival Process” (*J. Appl. Probab.* 47, 2010, DOI 10.1239/jap/1285335400), already constructs infinitely many distinct MAP2 parameterizations with identical full stationary observable laws; their 2012 weak-equivalence paper and Mészáros–Telek’s order-two canonical-representation work are also close. The explicit killed-reset \(q\)-interval, its physical endpoints, and its collapse on the exchange diagonal appear new, but they are a narrow feasibility calculation inside the classical similarity/nonidentifiability mechanism.

3. **DEPTH OF THE MATHEMATICS.** Modest: the headline proof is one-parameter \(2\times2\) similarity algebra followed by entrywise positivity inequalities; most remaining results assemble standard renewal, minimal-realization, confluent-Prony, LAN, delta-method, Hilbert-CLT, and Yurinskii machinery. The verification scripts are competent consistency checks, not mathematical depth or proof.

4. **TOP-JOURNAL VERDICT. TIER-4.** The original core is too model-specific and incremental, while the manuscript’s considerable length is dominated by technical specialization and bookkeeping rather than a new general mechanism.

5. **WHAT WOULD MOVE IT UP ONE TIER.** Prove, uniformly for \(z\) in compact subsets of \((0,1)\), the singular limit experiment at \(p=s=z\) under \(p_N=z+hN^{-1/4}\), \(s_N=z-hN^{-1/4}\), indexed by \(h^2\), together with matching minimax lower and upper bounds for testing/estimating \(|p-s|\) and an attaining record-based procedure; the current pointwise projection example is not such a theorem.

6. **WEAKEST LINK.** The compact-uniform calibration claim (U) in `thm:complete-markov-palm-tangent-omnibus-main`: its proof compresses the required triangular-array Hilbert-space CLT, growing truncation, trace-norm covariance control, and random renewal stopping into a short analytic argument, while the scripts verify only finite numerical instances; a referee is likely to demand a complete uniform proof.

Probab.* 47, 2010, DOI 10.1239/jap/1285335400), already constructs infinitely many distinct MAP2 parameterizations with identical full stationary observable laws; their 2012 weak-equivalence paper and Mészáros–Telek’s order-two canonical-representation work are also close. The explicit killed-reset \(q\)-interval, its physical endpoints, and its collapse on the exchange diagonal appear new, but they are a narrow feasibility calculation inside the classical similarity/nonidentifiability mechanism.

3. **DEPTH OF THE MATHEMATICS.** Modest: the headline proof is one-parameter \(2\times2\) similarity algebra followed by entrywise positivity inequalities; most remaining results assemble standard renewal, minimal-realization, confluent-Prony, LAN, delta-method, Hilbert-CLT, and Yurinskii machinery. The verification scripts are competent consistency checks, not mathematical depth or proof.

4. **TOP-JOURNAL VERDICT. TIER-4.** The original core is too model-specific and incremental, while the manuscript’s considerable length is dominated by technical specialization and bookkeeping rather than a new general mechanism.

5. **WHAT WOULD MOVE IT UP ONE TIER.** Prove, uniformly for \(z\) in compact subsets of \((0,1)\), the singular limit experiment at \(p=s=z\) under \(p_N=z+hN^{-1/4}\), \(s_N=z-hN^{-1/4}\), indexed by \(h^2\), together with matching minimax lower and upper bounds for testing/estimating \(|p-s|\) and an attaining record-based procedure; the current pointwise projection example is not such a theorem.

6. **WEAKEST LINK.** The compact-uniform calibration claim (U) in `thm:complete-markov-palm-tangent-omnibus-main`: its proof compresses the required triangular-array Hilbert-space CLT, growing truncation, trace-norm covariance control, and random renewal stopping into a short analytic argument, while the scripts verify only finite numerical instances; a referee is likely to demand a complete uniform proof.
